objectives: Distinguish definitely absent from possibly present in a Bloom filter.
Estimate filter memory and false-positive I/O under explicit assumptions.
Separate filter, page-cache, and compression effects in a storage budget.
retrieval: L042: why can one negative lookup encounter several sorted files?
L006: distinguish bits, bytes, decimal MB, and binary MiB.

sections.title: Avoid reading bytes that cannot answer the question
sections.markdown:
An LSM lookup for a missing key may examine many candidate files. Most contain nothing useful for that key. A small summary can reject impossible candidates before expensive block reads. The summary need not prove presence: it only needs a trustworthy negative result.

A Bloom filter is a bit array with several hash-derived positions for each inserted key. Insertion sets those positions. A query with any required bit unset is definitely absent from the represented set; if every bit is set, the key is only possibly present. Different keys can set the same positions, causing false positives. The actual index or data block must decide whether a possibly-present key exists.

sections.title: The guarantee depends on what the filter represents
sections.markdown:
For a correctly constructed filter queried with the same hash/encoding scheme, inserted elements are not false negatives. That conditional matters: an out-of-date filter, corruption, inconsistent normalization, or clearing shared bits can incorrectly reject a real key. The basic bit-array structure cannot safely delete a key by clearing its bits, because another key may depend on them. Immutable-file filters fit neatly: rebuild a filter for the replacement file during compaction.

With n inserted keys, m bits, and k approximately independent uniform hash positions per key, the usual false-positive approximation is p ≈ (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k. The approximate optimal k is (m/n) ln 2; choose a sensible integer in an implementation. This is a model, not a guarantee about an arbitrary toy hash. More bits reduce false positives but consume memory; more hashes add CPU and eventually stop helping.

Filter memory competes with index blocks, uncompressed data blocks, memtables, application memory, and operating-system caches. A cache stores data that has been read; a filter stores a lossy membership summary. Increasing one can force another out. Compare end-to-end I/O and latency under the real working set, not one metric in isolation.

sections.title: One million keys and a 1% target
sections.markdown:
For one million keys and target p=0.01, the approximation gives m = −n ln(p)/(ln 2)^2 ≈ 9.59 million bits, or 1.20 million bytes before allocation/metadata. That is about 1.14 MiB, with k ≈ 6.64, rounded to seven hash positions. It is not 9.59 MB: the formula returns bits.

Suppose a definitely-missing lookup checks eight independent candidate files, each with a 1% false-positive probability. The expected number of unnecessary file probes is 8 × 0.01 = 0.08. The chance of at least one false-positive file is approximately 1 − 0.99^8 ≈ 7.73%. These are different quantities. Independence is an approximation and a file probe is not automatically a physical disk operation when the needed block is cached.

Compression changes a different budget. If a requested 64-KiB uncompressed block occupies 20 KiB on disk, a cold miss reads fewer bytes but spends CPU decoding. If it is already cached uncompressed, that request may avoid both disk and decompression. A high-entropy encrypted blob may compress poorly; a repeated status column may compress well. Benchmark representative data and record whether cache sizes refer to compressed or uncompressed bytes.

sections.title: Executable estimation, then a failure experiment
sections.markdown:
The following arithmetic uses the approximation above. It does not allocate a filter and does not measure production false positives.

```python
from math import log, ceil

n, target = 1_000_000, 0.01
m = ceil(-n * log(target) / log(2) ** 2)
k = round(m / n * log(2))
print(m, k, round(m / 8 / 1024**2, 2))
assert 9_580_000 < m < 9_590_000
assert k == 7
assert round(1 - 0.99**8, 4) == 0.0773

```

Expected output is 9585059 7 1.14. To reason about unsafe deletion, imagine key A maps to bits {2,5} and key B maps to {5,7}. Inserting both sets 2,5,7. Deleting A by clearing 2 and 5 makes B fail its bit-5 check, even though B remains in the data. Rebuilding from the live set or using a carefully specified deletion-capable structure is required.

Common misconceptions: “possibly present” means found; 1% false positives means 1% of existing records disappear; compression saves CPU; and a large page cache rescues any access pattern. The filter only rejects negatives, compression trades resources, and caches need locality. Optional depth: account separately for a cold restart, where warm-cache measurements no longer describe the first reads.

sections.markdown: Core 55 minutes: 5 retrieval, 18 explanation and diagrams, 8 worked trace or arithmetic, 10 bounded exercise, 10 scheduled Q1–Q3, and 4 solution comparison/cards. Q4–Q5 and extension prompts are optional extra practice. Python blocks labeled executable are self-contained standard-library models; they do not implement a production storage engine.

diagrams.title: A negative filter answer can safely skip a file
diagrams.source:
flowchart LR
K[Lookup key] --> F[Bloom summary for file]
F -->|At least one bit unset| A[Skip file: absent]
F -->|All required bits set| I[Consult real file index]
I -->|Candidate block| C[Block cache lookup]
C -->|Miss| R[Read and decompress block]
C -->|Hit| V[Verify actual key and version]
R --> V
diagrams.caption: A Bloom-positive result is not a database answer. Data verification still decides presence and the visible version.
steps: Check membership bits using the same key encoding as insertion.
A definite negative removes a candidate file.
A positive continues through index and cache lookup.
Verify the actual key; a false positive simply did extra work.

exercise.prompt: A proposal allocates 10 bits/key for 20 million keys, with seven hash positions. Estimate raw filter MB, then expected unnecessary probes for six files at 1% false positives. Explain why clearing bits on deletion can break correctness using two overlapping keys.
rubric: Convert 200 million bits to 25 million bytes.
Distinguish expected probes 0.06 from probability of any false positive.
Use overlapping bits to demonstrate a false negative after unsafe deletion.
exercise.solution: 20,000,000 × 10 = 200,000,000 bits = 25,000,000 bytes, or 25 decimal MB before overhead. At six candidate files each with p=0.01, expected unnecessary probes are 0.06 per missing lookup; under independence the probability of at least one is 1−0.99^6≈5.85%. Keys A={2,5} and B={5,7} share bit 5. Clearing A’s bits removes bit 5 and falsely rejects B. Retain immutable-file filters until replacement or use a deletion-aware design with its own correctness argument.

questions.prompt: All Bloom query bits are set. What may the engine conclude?
options: The key may exist and needs verification
questions.answer: The key may exist and needs verification
questions.explanation: Collisions can set the same bits; membership is not proven by a positive.

questions.prompt: 20 million keys at 10 bits/key consume how many raw decimal MB?
What is unsafe in a basic Bloom filter?
options: Rebuilding it for a new immutable file
Clearing a removed key’s shared bit positions
Checking a real data block after a positive
questions.answer: Clearing a removed key’s shared bit positions
questions.explanation: Other still-present keys can depend on those bits, creating false negatives.

questions.prompt: Why might more Bloom memory make end-to-end performance worse?
questions.answer: It may displace useful cached data or indexes and add CPU work; evaluate the combined memory budget.
questions.explanation: Optimizing filter false-positive rate alone ignores the resource competition.

questions.prompt: Why is a 3× compression ratio not a 3× query speedup?
questions.answer: Some queries are CPU-bound, already cached, or read only a subset; decoding and metadata have costs.
questions.explanation: Fewer storage bytes is one mechanism, not an end-to-end latency equation.

flashcards.back: Definitely absent from the correctly represented set.

flashcards.front: Can basic Bloom bits be cleared safely for one deleted key?
flashcards.back: Not generally: bit positions may be shared.

flashcards.front: Ten bits per key in bytes?

flashcards.back: Filters reject impossible candidates; caches retain useful retrieved bytes.

mentalModel: Spend small, well-defined memory to avoid unnecessary I/O; never promote a probabilistic positive into truth.
